name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q01 - Matching thermodynamic processes with defining physical characteristics

questiontext.text:
Match the items in List I with the corresponding descriptions in List II:

List I (Process)List II (Feature)
A. Isothermal processII. Temperature remains constant throughout
B. Isochoric processIV. Volume remains constant and work done is zero
C. Isobaric processIII. Pressure remains constant and work is P(V₂ - V₁)
D. Adiabatic processI. No heat flows across boundaries (ΔQ = 0)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Characterization of an isothermal process
In an isothermal process, the temperature of the system is held strictly constant throughout the transformation (\(\Delta T = 0\)). For an ideal gas, pressure and volume vary inversely according to Boyle's law.

Step 2: Characterization of an isochoric process
In an isochoric process, the volume of the system is held constant (\(\Delta V = 0\)). Because the system boundaries do not move, the mechanical work done by or on the gas is identically zero (\(\Delta W = \int P dV = 0\)). All supplied heat goes directly into altering internal energy.

Step 3: Characterization of an isobaric process
In an isobaric process, the pressure is maintained constant during expansion or compression. The work performed by the gas against external pressure is directly given by \(W = P(V_2 - V_1) = \mu R(T_2 - T_1)\).

Step 4: Characterization of an adiabatic process
An adiabatic process is one in which the system is thermally insulated from its surroundings, preventing any heat exchange (\(\Delta Q = 0\)). Work done by the gas occurs entirely at the expense of its internal energy.

Step 5: Synthesis of all matching pairs
Isothermal process matches with constant temperature; Isochoric process matches with constant volume and zero work; Isobaric process matches with constant pressure work; and Adiabatic process matches with zero heat exchange.

Final Answer: Isothermal process pairs with constant temperature; Isochoric process pairs with constant volume and zero work; Isobaric process pairs with constant pressure work; and Adiabatic process pairs with zero heat exchange.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q02 - Matching thermodynamic quantities with their physical classifications

questiontext.text:
Match the items in List I with the corresponding descriptions in List II:

List I (Thermodynamic Quantity)List II (Classification)
A. PressureII. Intensive state variable representing normal force per unit area
B. Internal energyIII. Extensive state variable representing total molecular energy
C. Work doneIV. Path-dependent mode of mechanical energy transfer
D. TemperatureI. Intensive state variable determining thermal equilibrium

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of pressure
Pressure is an intensive state variable because its value does not scale with system size when a system in equilibrium is divided into sub-parts. It represents the macroscopic normal force exerted per unit area by the system constituents on the container walls.

Step 2: Classification of internal energy
Internal energy is an extensive state variable because it scales proportionally with the mass and size of the system. It represents the sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies in the rest frame of the center of mass, and its value is uniquely determined by the equilibrium state coordinates.

Step 3: Classification of work done
Work is not a state function; it is a path-dependent mode of energy transfer across boundaries brought about by macroscopic mechanical displacement of the boundary against resisting forces.

Step 4: Classification of temperature
Temperature is an intensive state variable that characterizes the condition of thermal equilibrium between systems, determining the spontaneous direction of heat flow when bodies are in thermal contact.

Step 5: Synthesis of all matching pairs
Pressure pairs with intensive state variable representing normal force per unit area; Internal energy pairs with extensive state variable representing total molecular energy; Work done pairs with path-dependent mode of mechanical energy transfer; and Temperature pairs with intensive state variable determining thermal equilibrium.

Final Answer: Pressure pairs with intensive force per unit area; Internal energy pairs with extensive state variable; Work done pairs with path-dependent energy transfer; and Temperature pairs with intensive variable determining thermal equilibrium.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q03 - Matching thermodynamic processes with work and energy equations

questiontext.text:
Match the items in List I with the corresponding descriptions in List II:

List I (Process)List II (Work / Energy Relation)
A. Isothermal expansionII. Q = W = μ R T ln(V₂ / V₁)
B. Adiabatic expansionI. W = μ R (T₁ - T₂) / (γ - 1)
C. Cyclic processIII. ΔU = 0 and W_net = Q_net
D. Isochoric heatingIV. W = 0 and ΔQ = ΔU = μ C_v ΔT

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Derivation of isothermal expansion work
For an ideal gas at constant temperature \(T\), internal energy is constant (\(\Delta U = 0\)). The work done in expanding from \(V_1\) to \(V_2\) is \(W = \int P dV = \mu R T \ln(V_2 / V_1)\). By the First Law of Thermodynamics, all absorbed heat equals the work performed: \(Q = W = \mu R T \ln(V_2 / V_1)\).

Step 2: Derivation of adiabatic expansion work
In an adiabatic process, heat exchange is zero (\(\Delta Q = 0\)). Integrating \(P dV\) using \(P V^\gamma = \text{constant}\) gives \(W = \frac{P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{\mu R (T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}\).

Step 3: Analysis of cyclic process relations
In any complete cyclic process, the system returns to its initial state coordinates, so the net change in internal energy over a complete cycle is zero (\(\Delta U = 0\)). By the First Law, the net work performed equals the net heat absorbed: \(W_{\text{net}} = Q_{\text{net}}\).

Step 4: Analysis of isochoric heating relations
In an isochoric process, volume remains fixed (\(dV = 0\)), so boundary work is zero (\(W = 0\)). All supplied heat increases internal energy: \(\Delta Q = \Delta U = \mu C_v \Delta T\).

Step 5: Synthesis of all matching pairs
Isothermal expansion pairs with \(Q = W = \mu R T \ln(V_2 / V_1)\); Adiabatic expansion pairs with \(W = \frac{\mu R (T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}\); Cyclic process pairs with \(\Delta U = 0\) and \(W_{\text{net}} = Q_{\text{net}}\); and Isochoric heating pairs with \(W = 0\) and \(\Delta Q = \Delta U = \mu C_v \Delta T\).

Final Answer: Isothermal expansion pairs with logarithmic work formula; Adiabatic expansion pairs with temperature-difference work formula; Cyclic process pairs with vanishing cyclic internal energy change; and Isochoric heating pairs with zero work and internal energy rise.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQ_Q04 - Matching Carnot cycle operations and second law concepts

questiontext.text:
Match the items in List I with the corresponding descriptions in List II:

List I (Carnot Stage / Concept)List II (Description / Governing Principle)
A. Step 1 → 2 of Carnot cycleII. Reversible isothermal expansion absorbing heat Q₁ at temperature T₁
B. Step 2 → 3 of Carnot cycleI. Reversible adiabatic expansion with temperature dropping from T₁ to T₂
C. Carnot engine efficiencyIV. η = 1 - (T₂ / T₁) independent of the nature of working substance
D. Kelvin-Planck statementIII. Denies complete cyclic conversion of absorbed heat into work

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analysis of Carnot Step 1 to 2
In the first step of the Carnot cycle, the working ideal gas undergoes a quasi-static reversible isothermal expansion at the source temperature \(T_1\), absorbing heat \(Q_1\) from the hot reservoir while performing mechanical work.

Step 2: Analysis of Carnot Step 2 to 3
In the second step, the gas is thermally insulated and undergoes a quasi-static reversible adiabatic expansion. The gas performs work at the expense of its internal energy, causing its temperature to decrease from source temperature \(T_1\) to sink temperature \(T_2\).

Step 3: Analysis of Carnot engine efficiency
The thermal efficiency of a reversible Carnot engine operating between temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) is given by \(\eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}\). According to Carnot's theorem, this efficiency is universal and completely independent of the working substance.

Step 4: Analysis of the Kelvin-Planck statement
The Kelvin-Planck statement of the Second Law of Thermodynamics establishes that no cyclic process is possible whose sole result is the absorption of heat from a single thermal reservoir and its complete conversion into work without rejecting heat to a cooler sink.

Step 5: Synthesis of all matching pairs
Step 1 to 2 pairs with reversible isothermal expansion; Step 2 to 3 pairs with reversible adiabatic expansion; Carnot engine efficiency pairs with \(\eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}\); and Kelvin-Planck statement pairs with the denial of complete cyclic conversion of heat to work.

Final Answer: Step 1 to 2 pairs with reversible isothermal expansion; Step 2 to 3 pairs with reversible adiabatic expansion; Carnot efficiency pairs with the temperature ratio formula; and Kelvin-Planck statement pairs with denying complete conversion of heat into work.
